::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Population Growth and Ultimate Value](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2554109/population-growth-and-ultimate-value), asked by [Cos Maths is a Sin](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/510033/cos-maths-is-a-sin) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2017-12-06; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> I was given this question and am unsure how to continue:
>
> ## Question
>
> > A population $x(t)$ grows in time according to
> > $\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} = (x-1)(2x-1)$. Knowing that
> > $x(0)=0$, after how much time does it reach $50\%$ of its ultimate
> > value as time passes?
>
> ## Attempt
>
> I first converted into partial fractions:
> $$\mathrm{d}t = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{(x-1)(2x-1)} \\
> \mathrm{d}t = \mathrm{d}x\left(\dfrac{1}{x-1} - \dfrac{2}{2x-1}\right)$$
>
> Then integrated to get
> $$t = \ln\left|x-1\right| - \ln\left|2x-1\right| + C$$
> Subbing in $x=0$ with $t=0$ (to determine $C=0$), then rearranging, I got:
> $$t = \ln\left|\dfrac{x-1}{2x-1}\right|$$
>
> My next instinct was to determine the maximum time, but after differentiating $t$ with respect to $x$, I get this, which has no solutions for $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}t}{\mathrm{d}x} = 0$:
> $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}t}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{(2x-1)(x-1)} = \dfrac{1}{x-1} - \dfrac{2}{2x-1}$$
>
> As you can see, I really just went in a circle. I don't know how to continue. Many thanks.
:::

> $$t = \ln\left|\dfrac{x-1}{2x-1}\right|$$

Looks good to me.

> My next instinct was to determine the maximum time,

Why?  Or more importantly, why should there be a “maximum time”?  The problem states:

>> after how much time does it reach $50\%$ of its ultimate value as time passes?

So think instead about finding $x_\infty = \lim_{t\to\infty} x(t)$, and then finding $t^*$ such that $x(t^*) = \frac{1}{2} x_\infty$.
